text:
Every load on a suspension bridge, from the heavy steel and asphalt of the roadway itself to the shifting weight of traffic and wind, begins its journey to the earth at the deck. Framing or lying beneath the road surface is a continuous stiffening truss or box girder. Instead of letting a heavy truck bend a small patch of roadway, this rigid structure spreads concentrated weights across a broader section of the span. Attached at regular intervals along the edges of the stiffening girder are vertical steel ropes called hangers or suspenders. The deck transfers both its own dead weight and the live loads of traffic outward to these hangers, pulling them taut in pure tension.

The upper ends of the hangers clamp onto the main suspension cables, which sweep high above the roadway from one end of the bridge to the other. Bound together from thousands of high-strength steel wires, these massive cables collect the downward pull from every hanger along the span. Because a flexible cable cannot support weight through stiffness or compression, it carries the entire suspended roadway through tension alone. Each hanger tugging downward adds to the internal pulling force running through the cable, redirecting the vertical weight sideways and upward along its sweeping curve. Guided by the uniform weight hanging beneath it, the main cable adopts a parabolic profile that channels these immense tensile stresses toward the primary supports.

At the peaks of the bridge's tall towers, the main cables rest inside heavy, curved steel housings called saddles. Here, the inward pull of the main span meets the outward pull of the side spans. Because the cable slopes downward on both sides of the saddle, the opposing horizontal forces largely balance one another, while the vertical pulls combine into a colossal downward push. In this way, the saddles convert the tensile pull of the cables into pure compression inside the towers. Acting as giant columns, the tower legs carry this crushing weight straight down through steel or reinforced concrete shafts. At the bottom, the towers rest on expansive concrete piers or deep caissons sunk beneath the riverbed or ground surface, spreading the immense compressive load onto solid bedrock or dense soil.

Yet the horizontal tension running through the main cables does not vanish at the towers; it continues down the sloping backstays toward the ends of the bridge. At both shorelines, each main cable fans out into smaller strands that connect to heavy steel eyebars buried inside colossal concrete blocks called anchorages. Unlike the towers, which endure downward crushing pressure, the anchorages resist a relentless upward and inward tug attempting to drag them toward the center of the bridge. Depending on local geology, engineers either build massive gravity anchorages whose sheer weight and friction against the earth resist sliding, or they tunnel directly into solid rock cliffs to lock the cables in place. By holding the cable ends immobile, the anchorages provide the final resistance for the suspended system, completing a continuous load path that guides every pound of weight safely into the ground.
